column1: A minimal model of money creation under regulatory constraints

The thesis titled A Minimal Model of Money Creation Under Regulatory Constraints by Victor Le Coz  Michael Benzaquen  and Damien Challet presents a minimal model of the secured interbank network to address recent puzzles in money markets. The authors identify that excess liquidity arises from the interactions between reserves and liquidity ratio constraints  leading to the emergence of evergreen repurchase agreements and collateral re-use as responses to banks' counterparty risk and liquidity ratio regulation. The model aligns with prevailing theories  suggesting that collateral re-use increases with scarcity. In this agent-based model  banks endogenously create money to meet the funding requests of economic agents  who generate payment shocks by reallocating their deposits. Banks absorb these shocks through repurchase agreements while adhering to reserves  liquidity  and leverage constraints. The resulting network is denser and more robust to stress scenarios than an unsecured one  and the stable bank trading relationships network exhibits a core-periphery structure. The model can be used for stress testing and monetary policy design.

The introduction highlights the motivation behind the study  noting that money markets are crucial for banks' refinancing operations and the money creation process  which provides liquidity to the financial system. The 2008 Great Financial Crisis (GFC) led to significant transformations in money markets  with the European Central Bank (ECB) introducing the full allotment procedure  allowing banks to request unlimited central bank funding. The Basel regulation's Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) aims to enhance banks' short-term resilience to liquidity crises by requiring them to maintain an adequate level of high-quality liquid assets. These measures have contributed to excess reserves in the financial system. The shift towards collateralized lending and the practice of collateral re-use have become prevalent  affecting the network structure of money markets.

The thesis reviews existing literature on interbank network modeling and introduces the agent-based model (ABM) developed by the authors. The model considers money creation and payment shocks within collateralized markets  subject to reserve  LCR  and leverage constraints. It explains excess liquidity and re-use through regulatory constraints and repo contracts specificities. The ABM generates a trading network with high density  stable bilateral trading relationships  asymmetric in– and out–degree distributions  and a core-periphery structure. The model serves as a tool for simulating systemic effects on financial stability during crisis scenarios or regulatory changes.

The section on money markets stylized facts presents observations that the ABM successfully reproduces. Following the GFC  the ECB's full allotment procedure led to a decline in the volumes of the overnight unsecured interbank market. The increase in excess liquidity between 2012 and 2018 was driven by banks' greater demand for central bank liquidity  the full allotment procedure  and longer-term refinancing operations. The ECB's asset purchase program (APP) further increased excess liquidity  with banks citing client inflows as the main reason. The introduction of the LCR in January 2018 reinforced the decline in unsecured lending. The combination of the APP and LCR constraint leads to excess liquidity in the financial system.

The thesis concludes by discussing the dynamical behavior of the model  the effects of parameter changes  and stress scenarios. The model provides insights into the systemic effects of crisis scenarios or regulatory changes on financial stability  offering a valuable tool for stress testing and monetary policy design.
